defaults.permitted_development: A driveway or other hard surface at a house in Wales is usually permitted development if it stays within the residential curtilage. Where the surface is in front of the principal elevation and between the house and the highway, hard surfacing over 5 square metres should be porous or permeable, or drain run-off to a porous area within the curtilage. A separate vehicular access or dropped-kerb approval may still be needed.

rules.height_rules: There is no standalone driveway height right. If the scheme needs significant embanking, terracing, retaining walls or steps, those elements may need planning permission in their own right.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth limit. The practical national test is whether the hard surface remains incidental to the house and, for front areas, whether drainage is handled correctly.
rules.boundary_rules: The works must stay within the curtilage. Forming a new access across a public footway, verge or roadside boundary normally needs highways consent and can also need planning permission, especially on classified roads or where rights have been removed.
rules.roof_rules: Driveways have no separate roof allowance. Car ports, canopies and garages are separate development types with their own rules.
rules.materials_rules: For front hard surfaces over 5 square metres between the house and the highway, use porous materials or direct water to a porous area in the curtilage. Small repairs to existing surfacing can be treated differently, but new works should be planned around drainage from the start.

rules.materials_rules: For front hard surfaces over 5 square metres between the house and the highway, use porous materials or direct run-off to a porous area within the curtilage. The design should keep water off the pavement and carriageway from the outset.

restrictions.conservation_area: In a conservation area, and especially where an Article 4 direction applies, front garden surfacing and boundary alterations are more sensitive and normal permitted development rights can be reduced or removed.
restrictions.listed_building: Works in the curtilage of a listed building are not treated as ordinary householder permitted development in Wales, and listed building consent may also be needed.

rules.permitted_development: A driveway or other hard surface at a house in Wales is often permitted development if it stays within the residential curtilage. In built-up streets, however, front garden parking still has to satisfy the porous surfacing rules, and a separate vehicular access or dropped-kerb approval may be needed before a car can lawfully cross the pavement.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate driveway height allowance. If the scheme needs notable terracing, retaining walls, ramps or steps, those elements can require their own planning assessment.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed national depth limit. In practice, the layout should be deep enough for a vehicle to stand on the site without overhanging the footway and should avoid forcing awkward reversing movements onto the road.

rules.permitted_development: A driveway or other hard surface at a house in Wales is usually permitted development if it stays within the residential curtilage. Where the surface is in front of the principal elevation and between the house and the highway, hard surfacing over 5 square metres should be porous or permeable, or drain run-off to a porous area within the curtilage. A separate vehicular access or dropped-kerb approval may still be needed.

rules.height_rules: There is no standalone driveway height right. If the scheme needs significant embanking, terracing, retaining walls or steps, those elements may need planning permission in their own right.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth limit. The practical national test is whether the hard surface remains incidental to the house and, for front areas, whether drainage is handled correctly.

rules.materials_rules: For front hard surfaces over 5 square metres between the house and the highway, use porous materials or direct water to a porous area in the curtilage. Small repairs to existing surfacing can be treated differently, but new works should be planned around drainage from the start.

rules.permitted_development: A driveway or hard surface at a house in Wales can still fall within national permitted development rules, but in a national park the practical question is often whether the works stay modest, preserve boundaries and avoid suburbanising a sensitive frontage. A separate access approval may still be needed.

rules.height_rules: There is no special driveway height right. Cut-and-fill work, embankments, retaining walls and raised platforms are more likely to move the proposal beyond a simple hard surface.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth limit, but extensive new parking courts or deep engineered platforms are less likely to read as minor incidental works in a protected landscape.
rules.boundary_rules: Removing stone walls, banks, verges or hedges to make access can be more significant than the surfacing itself. Even where the driveway area might be minor, the boundary changes can drive the planning outcome.
rules.roof_rules: Driveway rules do not cover roofed structures. Car ports, shelters and covered parking bays are separate development.
rules.materials_rules: Use permeable surfacing and subdued finishes. Bright suburban blockwork, heavy kerbing and over-engineered edging are more likely to attract objections in protected landscapes.
